Semiconductor companies describe industry cyclicality as a risk that limits their ability to maintain or improve net sales and profitability due to wide fluctuations in product supply and demand, often characterized by significant downturns. These downturns can result from factors such as maturing product cycles, excess inventories, declines in general economic conditions, and diminished product demand leading to production overcapacity and high inventory levels [1][2][4]. Companies note that these cyclical patterns cause substantial period-to-period fluctuations in operating results and may adversely affect their financial condition and results of operations [5]. Additionally, the timing, length, and severity of these up-and-down cycles are difficult to predict, which impacts a company's ability to accurately forecast future revenue and expense levels [3]. In response to downturns, companies may face increased competition for access to third-party foundry and assembly capacity, while significant upturns can lead to an inability to satisfy demand in a timely and cost-efficient manner [4].

Semiconductor companies describe their exposure to U.S. export controls as a significant risk that negatively impacts demand, supply chain complexity, margins, and competitive positioning. They cite specific business impacts including the need for increased compliance costs, potential diversion of customers to foreign competitors, inventory buildup due to purchase obligations, and limitations on market access.

Microchip Technology Inc (MCHP) notes that export controls may encourage non-U.S. customers to purchase from companies not subject to U.S. restrictions, harming their business and market position [1]. They also state that excessive controls increase the risk of investing in U.S. advanced semiconductor products because new products may be restricted before reaching the market [1].

Nvidia Corp (NVDA) highlights that export controls negatively impact demand not only in China but also in Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia [2]. They report that these controls can result in excess inventory and purchase obligations, citing their recent experience with the H20 product as an example [2]. Additionally, they note that complex controls impose burdensome compliance obligations on partners, suppliers, and customers, and that incorrect allegations regarding compliance satisfaction could damage their reputation [2].

Applied Materials Inc (AMAT) states that trade restrictions can increase supply chain complexity and manufacturing costs while decreasing margins and product competitiveness [3]. They specify that certain international sales depend on obtaining export licenses, and an inability to do so has limited their markets and negatively impacted revenues [3]. AMAT also mentions that U.S. export regulations for semiconductor technology sold in China have increased their exposure to foreign and Chinese domestic competition [3].

Advanced Micro Devices Inc (AMD) explains that export controls encourage customers in China and other markets to pursue alternatives to U.S. semiconductors to limit compliance burdens, affecting product roadmaps [4]. They note that changes to regulations or their interpretation could result in greater compliance costs and burdens on the business and its customers [4]. AMD also observes that governments may provide incentives like the CHIPS Act to benefit competitors, which could strengthen their relative position if such incentives are not available to AMD [4].

Teradyne, Inc (TER) describes how U.S. export restrictions have impacted sales to companies in China and manufacturing operations there [5]. They mention that while they mitigated some impact by obtaining licenses, new rules released in 2023 and 2024 continue to have an adverse impact on actual or potential customers and the global semiconductor industry [5]. Teradyne concludes that if these regulations disrupt the industry
